title: The d- and f-Block Elements: Chapter Introduction
summary: Iron bridges, copper wires and bright blue, purple and orange solutions all come from one part of the periodic table. The d-block (groups 3–12) fills d orbitals; the f-block (two rows below) fills f orbitals. Variable oxidation states, colour, magnetism and catalysis make them special.

notes.title: 01 – The d- and f-Block Elements: Chapter Introduction

keyPoints: **d-block**: the middle of the periodic table, **groups 3–12**; electrons fill the **d orbitals** (5 orbitals, up to 10 electrons).
**f-block**: two separate rows at the bottom, the **lanthanoids** (4f) and **actinoids** (5f); electrons fill the **f orbitals** (7 orbitals, up to 14 electrons).
Transition metals show **variable oxidation states**, form **coloured compounds**, are often **paramagnetic** and are good **catalysts**.
Everyday examples: iron (steel, bridges), copper (wires), blue CuSO₄, purple KMnO₄, orange K₂Cr₂O₇.

sections.h: Where the d- and f-blocks sit

blocks.p: The f-block is drawn separately so that the table stays compact: each f series has 14 elements.

list: **Variable oxidation states**: manganese shows every state from +2 to +7.
**Coloured compounds**: most transition-metal ions are coloured.
**Magnetism**: many ions have unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic.
**Catalysts**: iron in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the contact process, nickel in hydrogenation.
They also form complexes and alloys and have high melting points.
